title: VC1-06234
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.

The Appellant, XXXX XXXX (Mr. V) is a citizen of India. He fears that, if he returns to India, his former spouse's cousin will kill or seriously harm him. Mr. V is a Hindu man who married a Sikh woman in XXXX 2018. According to Mr. V, his wife's cousin XXXX (agent of persecution) came to his house in May 2018 and threatened to kill him. He alleges that XXXX is a gangster who is involved in drug trafficking. Mr. V also alleges that his former wife's family threatened to kill both her and Mr. V for the honour of the family. Mr. V left India for Canada in XXXX 2018 and made a refugee protection claim in early 2019.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that Mr. V would have a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Delhi, Mumbai, or Kolkata (IFA cities).

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 I do not agree with any of the reasons provided by Mr. V's representative as to why she believes the RPD erred in this case. The RPD was correct to find that Mr. V has a viable IFA in the IFA cities.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) only has the power to hold an oral hearing in certain circumstances in which it has admitted new evidence on appeal.2 As she does in all cases, Mr. V's representative has requested an oral hearing despite the fact that Mr. V has filed no new evidence on appeal. Mr. V's representative would do well to review the conditions for the holding of hearings by the RAD found in s. 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Mr. V has not submitted any new evidence on appeal. Therefore, I do not have the power to hold an oral hearing, and Mr. V's request for an oral hearing is denied. ANALYSIS ON THE MERITS No error in findings under the first prong of IFA test

The legal test for assessing whether a claimant has a viable IFA has two prongs.3 Under the first prong, the decision-maker assesses whether, on a balance of probabilities, the appellant would face a serious possibility of persecution in the IFA location or a likelihood that they would be subjected personally to any of the types of harm that would make them persons in need of protection there. I do not agree with Mr. V's representative that the RPD erred in finding that Mr. V would not face either a serious possibility of persecution, or a likelihood of serious harm, in the IFA cities.

Mr. V's representative argues that the agent of persecution could track Mr. V in the IFA cities due to the tenant verification system and police databases. She has made no arguments contesting the RPD's finding that Mr. V had failed to establish that the agent of persecution would have the motivation to track him down in the IFA cities. Since this finding is not contested, it is unnecessary for me to provide extensive reasons for why I agree with it. It suffices to say confirm that I have reviewed all of the evidence in this case and that I agree with the RPD's finding that Mr. V has failed to establish that the agent of persecution would have the motivation to track him down and persecute him in any of the IFA cities if he returned there today. I completely agree with the RPD's reasons on this issue and adopt them as my own.

In addition, I disagree with the arguments that Mr. V's representative has made about the means available to the agent of persecution to track Mr. V down in the IFA cities. In the appeal memorandum, Mr. V's representative has cut and pasted the arguments that she regularly makes regarding how Punjabi police are allegedly able to track claimants in IFA cities. Mr. V's representative has failed to take into consideration that the primary agent of persecution in this case, unlike in many other cases from India, is not the Punjabi police. Mr. V testified that the person he fears is his former wife's cousin. The only connection with the police was that Mr. V alleged that the cousin had connections with the police and political parties.

Mr. V alleged that, if he relocated to any of the IFA cities, he would have to submit to the tenant verification process and the Punjabi police would advise his former spouse's cousin or his accomplices about his location.4 I agree with the RPD that there was insufficient evidence in this case to establish that his former spouse's cousin or his accomplices would have the kinds of connections to the Punjabi police that would be required for the police to advise him of Mr. V's relocation to one of the IFA cities, if they ever did become aware of such a relocation. Therefore, I agree with the RPD that the agent of persecution would have the means to track Mr. V to one of the IFA cities if he relocates there today -- if he indeed would have the motivation to do so, which has not been established.

For all of the above reasons, I do not agree with the arguments made by Mr. V's representative as to why she believes the RPD erred under the first prong of the IFA test. I find that the RPD correctly concluded that Mr. V failed to establish that he would be subjected to either a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of serious harm if he relocates to one of the IFA cities. No error under the second prong of the IFA test

Under the second prong of the IFA test, a decision-maker must assess whether it would be unreasonable in all the circumstances to expect a claimant to relocate to one of the IFA cities. The threshold for unreasonableness is very high and requires that a claimant's life and safety be in jeopardy.5 For the reasons set out below, the RPD did not err in its analysis under the second prong of the IFA test.

I disagree with Mr. V's representative that the RPD failed to provide sufficient reasons to explain why the RPD relied upon the documentation it relied upon rather than the documents filed by Mr. V. In fact, Mr. V filed no documents in this case. It was Mr. V's onus to establish that any difficulties he might have finding employment in the IFA cities would be so serious as to put his life and safety in jeopardy. As noted by the RPD, Mr. V is a Hindu man in his 30s who managed a business in India and has also worked in Canada building custom cabinets and shower doors.

Although Mr. V's first language is Punjabi, the evidence in the National Documentation Package for India indicates that the three IFA cities are large multicultural cities in which many languages are spoken. There was insufficient evidence to establish that any language barrier Mr. V might encounter would be of such significance to make him unable to find employment in the IFA cities.

Finally, I do not agree with Mr. V's representative that the RPD erred in its conclusion that there were no factors relating to the Covid pandemic that would make it unreasonable to expect Mr. V to relocate to one of the IFA cities. The "arguments" made by Mr. V's representative take the form of assertions, such as the assertion that Mr. V would be disproportionately affected by the Covid pandemic. Mr. V's representative has made this argument without providing any explanation as to why she suggests that Mr. V disproportionately affected by the Covid pandemic other than to say that the pandemic would exacerbate the discrimination to which Mr. V is susceptible. I fail to see why this is the case. Mr. V is a Hindu man who previously was married to a Sikh woman. I do not find that the evidence establishes that anything relating to the Covid pandemic would have exacerbated any discrimination against him due to his situation. To the extent that Covid-related factors continue to exist in India today, the evidence does not establish that such factors would have any kind of disproportionate impact on Mr. V or any kind of adverse impact that would put his life and safety in jeopardy. RPD did not err in the assessment of documentary evidence

Mr. V's representative argues that the RPD erred in not giving sufficient weight to the documentary evidence filed by Mr. V. As noted above, Mr. V filed no evidence and therefore there is no basis for this argument, which appears to have simply been cut and pasted from previous appeal memoranda.

For the above reasons, the appeal is denied. I confirm the RPD's decision that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
